# How AI makes people confidently wrong

### The accuracy of people using AI drops by one-third, but their certainty that they’re right more than doubles.

SILICON VALLEY, CALIFORNIA (JULY 20, 2026) — New research published last week reveals the mechanism behind the workplace pandemic of people who are overconfident and underqualified.

The mechanism is fluency-based substitution: The ready availability of a syntactically coherent, decisive AI answer is accepted for its surface plausibility rather than because they fact-checked or verified the information (a process called “cognitive surrender”). The nature of AI answers lowers the threshold at which people judge they “know enough,” reducing a healthy suspension of judgment and inflating confidence in unverified information.

This dynamic partly explains the related pandemic of slop zombies.

As I told you in a recent piece , slop zombies are “people who use AI chatbots for everything. They bludgeon you with massively long, detailed, mediocre reports, messages, emails, and slide decks they didn’t even read (but expect you to read). They illustrate everything with AI slop and marvel at their own creativity.”

In that piece, I claimed that “slop zombies get dumber and lazier while their confidence rises. They believe the ideas and work of the AI chatbots are their own.”

Slop zombies delegate skepticism and judgment to the AI, which is often confidently wrong. Users then believe that the AI’s “knowledge” is their own.

#### The death of “I don’t know”

The study was conducted by researchers at three universities — the École Normale Supérieure in France, and Sapienza University of Rome and the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy.

The researchers found that when study participants had access to AI advice, their willingness to say “I don’t know” fell from 44% (close to half) to 3% (close to zero).

They didn’t say “I don’t know,” but in fact, they often didn’t know. With access to AI advice, participants’ accuracy fell from 27% to 9%. And their self-confidence rose from 30% to 76%.

In other words, the accuracy of people using AI was only one third, but they were more than twice as confident.

The mere availability of AI erodes the cognitive habit of recognizing what one does not know. In other words, AI makes people deluded about what they know and don’t know.

Prior Wharton research found something similar: People accept incorrect AI answers 80% of the time while reporting more confidence than those working without AI.

And that’s the biggest part of the slop zombie delusion: they’re super confident in their own knowledge and ability while actually not having much knowledge or ability. They become slop zombies when they act like they’re super-contributors.

Slop zombies spam co-workers with long, wordy and off-the-mark content, proposals, slide decks, emails believing themselves to be brilliant, when in fact they often lower productivity for the whole team or department because they make everyone else work harder to figure out which parts of their output are false or problematic.

Slop zombies are like someone operating a faulty tennis ball launcher and believing themselves to be Serena Williams.

The first step in dealing with the slop zombie contagion is learning to recognize a slop zombie when you see one. Also understand the phenomenon and mechanism of AI that deludes people into confidently asserting false information as true and their own.

Check out my previous piece on slop zombies for specific advice on what you can do about the slop zombies walking among us.

# If AI companies avoid AI slop, shouldn't we?

### AI companies expect us to consume AI-generated content, even though they themselves vastly prefer human-generated content for training AI models.

SILICON VALLEY, CALIFORNIA (JULY 23, 2026) — 404 Media reported recently that AI companies are buying pre-AI books for training AI.

One major source for book data is a company called ISBNdb, which started out as a source of book metadata for libraries and book sellers, then pivoted to also offering digitized books for training AI. The company claims to be the world’s largest repository of book data and contains around 111 million books.

ISBNdb says that books printed before 2022 largely don’t contain AI-generated content, and are therefore coveted for AI training.

AI companies are also especially keen on Reddit data . One of the reasons for that is that much of that content is generated by people, rather than AI. (They also like it because the topics are many, the information is always being updated and the voting system provides the bonus of human-judgment on the quality of the information.)

While AI companies are flooding the world with AI-generated content, they themselves try to avoid it. The main worry is a fear of “model collapse,” which is what happens when AI is trained on AI data.

“Model collapse” is the process of declining accuracy and quality of output as AI models are trained on multiple generations of AI-generated content. With AI trained on AI content, rare or unusual ideas get lost, the output becomes more generic and average, and hallucinations get validated as true, leading to their elevation in the possible answers chatbots give.

#### Here’s the problem

But what’s the difference between AI training data generated by humans who get their information from AI? “Model collapse” still happens — in fact, it’s already happening — but with people plugged into the process.

When a generation of content by writers using AI gets fed back into the system to train AI, then that AI training is pushed back out to writers, who write based on AI-influenced AI and churn out even more homogenized works, and then that content is then fed back into the system, you can see how “model collapse” works even when people are involved.

One study looked at part of the phenomenon. They found that AI-generated story ideas improved the creativity of individual writers, but made the ideas converge with those of other writers using AI to generate ideas, homogenizing the totality of stories (just like in “model collapse”). This study and this also came to similar conclusions.

These studies focused on decreased creativity and diversity of opinion and ideas. But they didn’t address human mediated AI “model collapse.”

It’s nice to see what companies like Substack are doing. (Note: This newsletter is published on Substack.)

# Rise of the 'slop zombies'

### Corporate America and the wider world of work are suffering from a pandemic of AI-pilled slop zombies infected with brain rot and unearned confidence.

SILICON VALLEY, CALIFORNIA (JULY 10, 2026) — If you have a job in 2026, you know the type.

I’m talking about people who use AI chatbots for everything. They bludgeon you with massively long, detailed, mediocre reports, messages, emails, and slide decks they didn’t even read (but expect you to read). They illustrate everything with AI slop and marvel at their own creativity.

Churning out long, complicated missives with AI forces others in the company to use AI to keep up. The slop zombie virus is contagious.

Because of the low time and cognitive cost of producing AI-generated communications, and because AI chatbots by default tend to be extremely wordy and detailed, they incentivize you to use AI to boil down the slop zombies’ bloated content. People end up functioning as mere couriers of messages between AI chatbots.

As the habit sets in to use AI for everything, slop zombies get dumber and lazier while their confidence rises. They believe the ideas and work of the AI chatbots is their own. As chatbots churn out often false or hallucinatory junk with confidence , so do the slop zombies.

Developers using Claude Code or some other tool are filled with certainty about the quality of their work, bickering with other developer slop zombies who are equally confident and equally unfamiliar with the code they’re arguing about.

“Imposter mode,” whereby someone who is actually qualified feels unqualified, has been replaced by “slop zombie imposter mode,” whereby someone actually unqualified feels overqualified. Slop zombies feel that way because they mistake chatbot flattery and sycophancy for earned praise, and also because of the delusion that AI output is their own work.

A disproportionate number of bosses have become AI-pilled slop zombies, using AI to run companies or departments and even mandating that everyone over-rely on AI.

One slop zombie trait is to devalue feedback from people to the point of being dismissive of any human-generated ideas, and overvalue chatbot output, thus spreading the contagion.

AI is supposed to boost productivity. But slop zombies are killing it. When you work with a slop zombie, you waste all your time pouring over mountains of chatbot output in the form of long-winded reports or vibe-coded software packed with errors and hallucinations and off-topic ideas that are cognitively draining to find and expose. It’s a slop tax on productivity.

Slop zombies offload not only cognitive tasks to AI, but social skills and emotional intelligence. People are consoling co-workers and even firing people using words generated by AI chatbots. They use a machine to sound more human.

Slop zombies are the new office menace. But what is to be done?

#### The trouble with slop zombies

Like regular zombies, slop zombies feed on human brains (in the form of LLM training data), yet suffer from personal brain rot.

They don’t realize that they’re not fully participating in their own lives anymore.

The worst part is that they believe themselves to be the opposite of what they are:

- Obsessive over-dependence on AI chatbots has made them far dumber and far less productive, but they believe themselves to be super smart and highly productive.

- They believe themselves to be full of great ideas, but they’ve outsource idea-making to the machines.

- They believe themselves to be super valuable to the company, but in fact have already replaced themselves with AI and are therefore in fact of little value.

To accuse a boss or co-worker of being a slop zombie is hard to do. They’ll deny it because it strikes at the core of their professional identity, and because in any event, they don’t believe it.

Unlike in academia, where professors can test students with oral presentations and zero-AI test settings, it’s hard to prove that a co-worker didn’t do the work.

Also: The difference between a smart user of AI who uses it to become smarter on the one hand, and a slop zombie on the other, is actually hard to spot.

Is someone using AI to offer options to consider, or are they just copying and pasting ideas from chatbots? Superficially, it’s a fine line. In reality, the distinction is everything. Here are the differences between a smart user of AI and a slop zombie:

- The smart user can explain why they chose this output over the alternatives the AI offered. The slop zombie can’t, because they never considered alternatives.

- The smart user modifies, rejects, or overrides AI output based on domain knowledge the AI doesn’t have. The slop zombie presents it verbatim (or near-verbatim with superficial edits).

- The smart user’s work improves over time because the AI interaction helps sharpen their thinking. The slop zombie’s work degrades over time because they’re outsourcing the thinking itself, which weakens cognition.

- The smart user gets less dependent on AI as they learn more. The slop zombie gets more dependent.
